title: 9/8/2026 | Clare Nelson | LTRS | Security. On Jul 22, CISA, FBI warned that Iranian-affiliated cyber actors are exploiting PLCs across U.S. critical infrastructure. Days later, US water treatment was hacked. This is my PUC testimony from Aug 14. Security vulns are reason to stop 765.

=== PUC Testimony.pdf ===
                                    Testimony of Clare Nelson
                              (Retired Cybersecurity Professional)
                       Public Utility Commission of Texas Public Meeting
                                         August 14, 2026

Good morning, Chairman Gleeson and Commissioners.

My name is Clare Nelson, I’m an affected landowner for the Bell County East – Big Hill
line.

I am a cybersecurity professional with certifications in information security, data privacy, and
cloud technology. I also served on the Board of Directors of the Austin Chapter of the
Information Systems Security Association.

Even though I am retired, I still get nightmares. We are vulnerable to attacks, and nation
states keep upping their game.

On July 22, 2026, CISA, FBI, EPA, and other U.S. Government partners updated a joint
cybersecurity advisory warning that Iranian-affiliated cyber actors are exploiting
Programmable Logic Controllers, or PLCs, across U.S. critical infrastructure.

Days later, water and wastewater utilities in at least twelve states reported cyberattacks
targeting operational technology (OT). Attackers targeted internet-connected PLCs, changing
IP addresses and passwords and, in some cases, disrupting operators’ ability to monitor and
control critical systems. The attacks caused loss of water pressure, flooding, and operational
disruptions across multiple states, including a precautionary boil-water advisory affecting
customers in Georgia. Investigators are examining possible Iranian involvement.

The lesson applies directly to the electric grid. Texas relies on tens of thousands of industrial
control devices, including PLCs, protective relays, Remote Terminal Units (RTUs), and other
automation controllers. Each improperly secured connected device can become a potential
cyberattack pathway.

The Texas Legislature has already recognized these risks through the Texas Grid Security Act,
SB 75, and the Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act, SB 2116.

As the Commission oversees development of new electric infrastructure across Texas, I
encourage you to make cybersecurity a core element of reliability planning. That means rigorous
cybersecurity standards, resilience against cyber and physical attacks, and independent
verification of supply-chain security—not just attestations.

If I told you this iPhone contains no parts from China, would you simply take my word for it? Of
course not. You would expect independent verification. Texas should apply that same standard
to critical grid infrastructure.
 The recent attacks on water utilities should serve as a warning. We have the opportunity to apply
those lessons before, not after, a major cyber incident affects Texas electric infrastructure.

I respectfully ask the Commission to make cybersecurity and independent verification
foundational requirements for every major grid investment.

Electricity is not reliable if the grid is not secure.

Thank you.
